# Simulation with Verilator

[]{#ref-verilator .reference-destination}

## Concepts

### What Verilator does

Verilator is an open-source compiler for Verilog and SystemVerilog models. It checks RTL and translates supported constructs into C++ or SystemC. A native compiler then builds an executable that performs the simulation. The build and simulation are separate stages: editing the RTL requires rebuilding the executable.

@fig-verilator-flow shows the two stages for the accumulator used in this chapter.

![Build and run flow of the accumulator example. Verilator translates the RTL into a C++ model, a C++ compiler builds it together with the harness, and the executable reports a result and writes a trace. A warning under -Wall stops the build before any simulation.](../../figures/verilator-build-and-run.svg){#fig-verilator-flow width=100% fig-alt="Verilator, generated C++ model, compiler, executable and result for the accumulator example"}

In a C++ flow, the test harness supplies inputs, clock transitions, and checks. The generated model exposes top-level ports, and `eval()` evaluates its behavior. Tracing can record waveforms for debugging. See the official [overview](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/overview.html) and [model API guide](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/connecting.html).

This chapter develops an original clocked accumulator example. It follows the create–compile–run progression of the official [C++ example](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/example_cc.html), adding reset, enable, overflow checks, and a reference model. Consult the [user guide](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/index.html) for the installed version's supported constructs.

### What Verilator does not model

Verilator simulates a two-state, cycle-oriented model of your RTL, which is what makes it fast. A signal is 0 or 1 at every evaluation, so an uninitialized register shows a value instead of an `X`, and how it is initialized is an option you choose; the [user guide](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/index.html) documents the choices [@verificationVerilator]. HDL delay controls need `--timing`, and even then they schedule simulation events and are not gate or wire delays. The model also shows only settled values at each evaluation, so glitches and races that a gate-level simulation could expose stay invisible. None of this is a defect. It means Verilator answers "is the cycle-level behavior right?" very well, and questions about unknown values, reset release or timing need another tool, such as the four-state Icarus runs in the [cocotb chapter](cocotb.qmd) or static timing analysis.

### The experiment's hardware contract

The accumulator uses a rising-edge clock and unsigned 16-bit operands:

| Condition at the rising edge | Sum after the edge | Valid | Overflow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reset or clear asserted | Zero | Zero | Zero |
| Enable asserted | Previous sum plus operand, modulo 65536 | One | One if addition exceeds 65535 |
| Otherwise | Previous sum retained | Zero | Zero |

Reset and clear have priority over enable. Valid marks an accepted addition, not merely a nonzero stored result. Overflow is a one-cycle report for an addition; it is not a sticky flag.

The C++ reference uses a wider integer and explicit modulo arithmetic. It checks every cycle, including stalls and resets, rather than treating a plausible waveform as a passing test.

### The simulator's place in the verification plan

The C++ scoreboard below checks numerical and control behavior at unit level, under the contract in @sec-verification-methodology. Waveforms are the quickest way to understand the first failure, but a PASS vouches only for the scenarios that ran. Keep the automatic comparisons, the timeout and the failing exit status when you add traces or random traffic, so a broken run cannot look like a quiet one. Look at each warning on its merits: a build that tolerates warnings is not a clean lint result. Record the initialization/X-handling and assertion options you used, since they change what a PASS means. Code coverage is a good pointer to logic your tests never reached, but functional bins from the contract and an independent oracle still decide whether the behavior is right [@verificationVerilator].


## Implementation

**Recipe status:** the supplied one-operand RTL/C++ build and 14-cycle check are a **checked recipe** (Verilator 5.020 baseline), and so are the faulty variants and the 17-vector extension in the sections that follow. Installation/source-build choices are **adaptation templates**; width/random-stimulus changes are **exercises**. Keep the stated example working directory, or use the root-level `verilator` lab entry.


### Download the example files

- [accumulator.sv](../../examples/verilator/accumulator.sv): SystemVerilog design.
- [sim_main.cpp](../../examples/verilator/sim_main.cpp): C++ test harness.

Save both files in the same directory, keeping their filenames. If your browser displays a file as text, use **Save link as** to download it. Run the commands below locally in that directory.

### Install the tools

On Ubuntu or Debian, install the packaged tool and a C++ build environment:

```sh
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y verilator build-essential
verilator --version
g++ --version
make --version
```

On Windows, use Ubuntu under WSL2 for this walkthrough. From an administrator PowerShell terminal:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
```

Complete setup, restart if requested, and run the Linux commands inside Ubuntu. The native Windows toolchain is another option, but requires a different setup. Packaged versions may lag newer releases. The official [installation guide](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/install.html) also describes source builds:

```sh
sudo apt-get install -y git help2man perl python3 make autoconf g++ flex bison
git clone https://github.com/verilator/verilator.git
cd verilator
git checkout stable
unset VERILATOR_ROOT
autoconf
./configure
make -j2
sudo make install
verilator --version
git describe --tags --always
```

For reproducibility, replace `stable` with a selected release tag and record it. For package/global installations, leave `VERILATOR_ROOT` unset.

### Prepare a working directory

The two source files are included in this book repository under `examples/verilator/`. In a Linux or WSL terminal, from the repository root:

```sh
cd examples/verilator
ls accumulator.sv sim_main.cpp
```

For an independent exercise, create a directory with `mkdir verilator-accumulator`, enter it, and save the following two listings using the exact filenames shown. Use LF line endings.

### Describe the circuit: accumulator.sv

```systemverilog
module accumulator(
  input  logic        clk, reset, Clear, Enable,
  input  logic [15:0] Operand,
  output logic [15:0] Sum,
  output logic        Valid, Overflow);

  logic [16:0] ExtendedSum;
  assign ExtendedSum = {1'b0, Sum} + {1'b0, Operand};

  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset || Clear) begin
      Sum      <= '0;
      Valid    <= 1'b0;
      Overflow <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      Valid    <= Enable;
      Overflow <= Enable && ExtendedSum[16];
      if (Enable) Sum <= ExtendedSum[15:0];
    end
  end
endmodule
```

The addition explicitly extends both operands to 17 bits, preserving the carry. Only the low 16 bits enter the sum register. The clocked process updates state with nonblocking assignments, and the default branch clears the reporting flags on a disabled cycle.

### Write the C++ harness: sim_main.cpp

```cpp
#include "Vaccumulator.h"
#include "verilated.h"
#include "verilated_vcd_c.h"

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

struct Stimulus {
    bool reset;
    bool clear;
    bool enable;
    std::uint16_t operand;
};

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    VerilatedContext context;
    context.commandArgs(argc, argv);
    context.traceEverOn(true);
    Vaccumulator dut{&context};
    VerilatedVcdC trace;
    dut.trace(&trace, 3);
    trace.open("accumulator.vcd");
    if (!trace.isOpen()) {
        std::cerr << "Cannot open accumulator.vcd\n";
        dut.final();
        return 1;
    }

    dut.clk = 0;
    dut.reset = 1;
    dut.Clear = 0;
    dut.Enable = 0;
    dut.Operand = 0;

    // Each sample has a distinct timestamp: low, rising edge, falling edge.
    auto evaluate = [&]() {
        dut.eval();
        trace.dump(context.time());
        context.timeInc(5);
    };

    const std::array<Stimulus, 14> tests{{
        {true,  false, false,     0}, // Reset.
        {true,  false, true,     99}, // Reset wins over enable.
        {false, false, true,      5},
        {false, false, true,      9},
        {false, false, false, 12345}, // Hold sum; valid/overflow low.
        {false, true,  true,    100}, // Clear wins over enable.
        {false, false, true,  60000},
        {false, false, true,  10000}, // 70000 wraps to 4464.
        {false, false, false,     7}, // Overflow must not stay asserted.
        {false, false, true,  65535}, // Another wrap.
        {false, true,  false,     0},
        {false, false, true,  65535}, // Exact maximum; no overflow.
        {false, false, true,      1}, // Wrap to zero.
        {true,  false, true,      3}  // Reset nonzero/overflow state.
    }};

    std::uint32_t expected_sum = 0;
    unsigned failures = 0;
    unsigned cycle = 0;
    for (const auto& input : tests) {
        dut.reset = input.reset;
        dut.Clear = input.clear;
        dut.Enable = input.enable;
        dut.Operand = input.operand;
        dut.clk = 0;
        evaluate(); // Settle inputs before the active edge.

        bool expected_valid = false;
        bool expected_overflow = false;
        if (input.reset || input.clear) {
            expected_sum = 0;
        } else if (input.enable) {
            const std::uint32_t total = expected_sum + input.operand;
            expected_sum = total % 65536u;
            expected_overflow = total >= 65536u;
            expected_valid = true;
        }

        dut.clk = 1;
        evaluate(); // Commit the clocked updates before checking outputs.
        if (dut.Sum != expected_sum
            || static_cast<bool>(dut.Valid) != expected_valid
            || static_cast<bool>(dut.Overflow) != expected_overflow) {
            ++failures;
            std::cerr << "FAIL cycle " << cycle
                      << ": sum=" << dut.Sum << " expected=" << expected_sum
                      << ", valid=" << unsigned(dut.Valid)
                      << " expected=" << expected_valid
                      << ", overflow=" << unsigned(dut.Overflow)
                      << " expected=" << expected_overflow << '\n';
        }

        dut.clk = 0;
        evaluate();
        ++cycle;
    }

    dut.final();
    trace.close();
    if (failures != 0) return 1;
    std::cout << "PASS: " << cycle << " cycles checked\n";
    return 0;
}
```

The generated class is `Vaccumulator`. `VerilatedContext` owns simulation context and time; the harness passes command-line arguments to it. `final()` completes model finalization. `VerilatedVcdC` records a VCD file after tracing is enabled. These APIs are described in [Connecting to Verilated Models](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/connecting.html).

Each cycle has three evaluations. First, drive the inputs with the clock low and settle the combinational addition. Next, raise the clock, evaluate the state transition, and compare outputs. Finally, lower the clock and evaluate again. All samples have different timestamps.

The test avoids checking old values before clocked updates are evaluated. Its reference calculation is independent of the RTL's carry extraction. A mismatch prints actual and expected values and returns a nonzero exit status. The fixed 14-cycle sequence guarantees termination; the RTL does not need `$finish`.

No HDL delay controls are used, so this harness does not require `--timing`. Advancing context time alone does not toggle the clock: the assignments and `eval()` calls do that. The five-unit increments label waveform phases; they do not model gate delays or establish timing closure.

## Hands-on Experiments

### Compile the model and harness

[Core option · P2 · C1](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-verilator-baseline .learning-activity}

From the directory containing the two files:

```sh
verilator --cc --exe --build -j 2 -Wall --trace \
  --top-module accumulator -CFLAGS "-std=c++17" \
  sim_main.cpp accumulator.sv
```

| Option | Role in this build |
| --- | --- |
| `--cc` | Generate C++ model sources |
| `--exe` | Include the supplied C++ harness in an executable build |
| `--build` | Invoke the generated build rules |
| `-j 2` | Limit build parallelism to two jobs |
| `-Wall` | Enable additional warnings |
| `--trace` | Include waveform-tracing support |
| `--top-module accumulator` | Select the intended top module |
| `-CFLAGS "-std=c++17"` | Select C++17 for the C++ compilation |

The translation/build flow follows the official [C++ walkthrough](https://verilator.org/guide/latest/example_cc.html). Inspect warnings rather than disabling them indiscriminately. Generated sources and the executable are placed in `obj_dir/`.

### Reading the generated model

The build leaves the generated C++ and the executable in `obj_dir/`. Open `Vaccumulator.h` to see what your harness can touch: each port is a public member, `Enable` declared as `VL_IN8(&Enable,0,0)` and `Operand` as `VL_IN16(&Operand,15,0)`, so one-bit ports occupy a byte and the 16-bit ports a 16-bit integer. The class also declares `eval()` and `final()`, the two calls the harness uses to advance and finish the model. Knowing where the ports come from makes a compile error in the harness easy to read, and it is the first thing to check when you change a width.

### Run and inspect the result

```sh
./obj_dir/Vaccumulator
echo $?
```

Expected output:

```text
PASS: 14 cycles checked
```

The exit status should be zero. This example was compiled and executed with Verilator 5.020 in a Linux container, passing all 14 checks. For example, adding 10000 to 60000 produces sum 4464 and an overflow pulse. The following disabled cycle must preserve 4464 while clearing both reporting flags. Reaching exactly 65535 must not report overflow; adding one afterward must wrap to zero.

The run creates `accumulator.vcd` in the current working directory. Open it with a VCD viewer, such as GTKWave if installed:

```sh
gtkwave accumulator.vcd
```

Inspect `clk`, `reset`, `Clear`, `Enable`, `Operand`, `Sum`, `Valid`, and `Overflow`. Use the waveform to explain a failed check, while retaining the automatic reference comparison as the pass criterion. Generated files are excluded by the example's local `.gitignore`.

### Break the design on purpose

A test that has never failed has never shown it can. Exercise 1 asks you to break the overflow logic; here is what that looks like. In `accumulator.sv`, replace the overflow assignment with one that also reports the exact maximum:

```systemverilog
Overflow <= Enable && (ExtendedSum >= 17'd65535);
```

Rebuild and run. The harness prints one line for the failing cycle and exits with status 1:

```text
FAIL cycle 11: sum=65535 expected=65535, valid=1 expected=1, overflow=1 expected=0
```

Read it from the left. Cycles count from zero, so this is the twelfth vector, the one commented "Exact maximum; no overflow". The sum and `Valid` agree with the reference and only `Overflow` differs, so the fault is in how overflow is derived and not in the adder. Open `accumulator.vcd` at that rising edge: `Operand` is 65535, `Sum` was cleared, and the mutant raises `Overflow` for a total of 65535 that fits in 16 bits. Restore the original line, rebuild, and the run is back to `PASS: 14 cycles checked`. Only that one cycle failed, which is what a good check should do: point at the vector and the signal.

### A test that passes and should not

Two other faults look just as plausible. In the first, overflow ignores `Enable`:

```systemverilog
Overflow <= ExtendedSum[16];
```

In the second, `Valid` also requires a nonzero operand:

```systemverilog
Valid    <= Enable && (Operand != 0);
```

Build each one. Both print `PASS: 14 cycles checked`. The test is green and the design is wrong, because none of the 14 vectors drives the situations these faults change: a disabled cycle whose operand would produce a carry, and an enabled cycle with a zero operand. Add three vectors before the final reset vector and change the array size from 14 to 17:

```cpp
        {false, false, true,  40000}, // Sum becomes nonzero.
        {false, false, false, 40000}, // Disabled: a carry here must not report overflow.
        {false, false, true,      0}, // Enabled zero operand is still a valid addition.
```

```cpp
    const std::array<Stimulus, 17> tests{{
```

The unmodified RTL still passes, with `PASS: 17 cycles checked`, and the two faults now fail:

```text
FAIL cycle 14: sum=40000 expected=40000, valid=0 expected=0, overflow=1 expected=0
FAIL cycle 15: sum=40000 expected=40000, valid=0 expected=1, overflow=0 expected=0
```

The lesson is about the vectors and not about these two faults. A hand-written list covers the cases its author thought of, and the survivors were cases nobody had thought of. A seeded pseudo-random sequence (Exercise 3) finds gaps like these without being told where to look, and the functional bins in @sec-verification-methodology state in advance what must be exercised. A green run, therefore, reports only on the scenarios that ran.

| Fault introduced | 14 vectors | 17 vectors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overflow also at exactly 65535 | fails | fails |
| Overflow never clears | fails | fails |
| Overflow ignores `Enable` | **passes** | fails |
| `Valid` requires a nonzero operand | **passes** | fails |
| `Clear` ignored | build stops at lint | build stops at lint |

This table is a **checked recipe**. `python labs/run.py run verilator` builds every variant from [mutation_check.py](../../labs/05-verification/mutation_check.py) against both harnesses and fails if any outcome differs from the table.

### Let lint speak first

The last fault never reaches simulation. Remove `Clear` from the reset condition:

```systemverilog
if (reset) begin
```

The build stops, because `-Wall` enables this warning and Verilator treats warnings as fatal unless told otherwise:

```text
%Warning-UNUSEDSIGNAL: accumulator.sv:2:35: Signal is not used: 'Clear'
%Error: Exiting due to 1 warning(s)
```

Verilator found a real bug at build time, before any waveform or vector. That is the reason to read each warning on its merits and not to silence the tool. If a warning is a deliberate choice, waive it narrowly with a comment that says why, at the exact line, so the next reader sees the decision; the policy in @sec-verification-methodology explains why a global `-Wno-fatal` hides new defects.

### Extend the checks

1. [Core option · P2 · C1](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-verilator-01 .learning-activity} — Change the RTL overflow test deliberately so that exactly 65535 reports overflow. Rebuild and confirm that the test fails.
2. [Core option · P2 · C1](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-verilator-02 .learning-activity} — Add consecutive disabled cycles after a wrap and check that overflow never becomes sticky.
3. [Core option · P2 · C1](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-verilator-03 .learning-activity} — Replace the fixed stimulus with a deterministic pseudo-random sequence while retaining the reference calculation and a cycle limit.
4. [Core option · P2 · C1](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-verilator-04 .learning-activity} — Add a test that changes inputs while the clock remains low. Verify that the sum register changes only on a rising edge.
5. [Core option · P2 · C1](../../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-verilator-05 .learning-activity} — Parameterize the width and update the C++ interface/reference arithmetic accordingly. Do not assume wide ports have the same generated C++ representation as this 16-bit example.

Record tool versions, source revision, command, exit status, and any failing cycle. This exercise checks a small synchronous block; processor simulation adds memory models, software loading, and architectural-state checks.

<!-- chapter-review:verilator -->

## Key ideas {#review-verilator-ideas .unnumbered .unlisted}

- Verilator turns supported RTL into an executable simulation model, so every RTL edit needs a rebuild.
- The C++ harness supplies stimulus, clock progression and checking.
- A passing run covers only the vectors it ran; breaking the design on purpose shows what the test can and cannot detect.

## What you should now be able to explain {#review-verilator-explain .unnumbered .unlisted}

Explain one simulation iteration, including signal updates, evaluation, sampling and the scoreboard decision, and name one fault the 14-vector test misses and the vector that exposes it.

## Common mistakes {#review-verilator-mistakes .unnumbered .unlisted}

Two traps catch most newcomers. A model that builds has only shown that the RTL can be translated, not that it is correct. And sampling before the model reflects the intended clock edge shifts every check by one cycle, which can make a correct design look broken or a broken one look right.
